titulo.texto: Sacred Yarn Nierika (Vision and Path to Wirikuta)

frase_gancho.texto: A yarn painting that is, for the person who makes it, a doorway.

puente_narrativo.texto: These same people dress in the story the painting tells. Look for a white cotton outfit, with shirt, trousers, shoulder bags and a hat adorned with feathers, all embroidered with deer and flowers.

guion_corto.texto: This yarn painting is a nierika, a sacred object of the Wixárika (Huichol) people. It is made by pressing colored yarn, strand by strand, onto a board covered with wax and resin. It is not a decoration: it is an offering and a way of seeing. It tells of the journey to Wirikuta, a sacred desert in San Luis Potosí, hundreds of kilometers from the mountains, where the Wixárika make a pilgrimage every year to seek the peyote. Look for the blue deer, Kauyumari, who guides the way; for the fire, Tatewari, the oldest grandfather; for the sun and the peyote flowers. Every color shines because every vision matters, and every thread counts.

guion_largo.texto:
A nierika looks like a painting, but for the person who makes it, it is more like a doorway. It is usually linked to the word “to see”; some explanations translate it as “face” or “mirror.” It is not made to decorate a wall. It is made to offer to the gods and to show what was seen in a ceremony. That you see it today in a museum does not change what it is.

The process takes enormous patience. A board is prepared with a layer of wax and resin, which is warmed a little so that it becomes sticky. Then the design is drawn, and the colored yarn is pressed onto the wax, thread by thread. One of these paintings can take you weeks. Starting in the 1960s, it also became a form of art that is sold, and it has helped many families.

What does it tell? A journey. Every year, groups of Wixárika make a pilgrimage to Wirikuta, a desert in San Luis Potosí, hundreds of kilometers from their mountains. There, according to their account, the first Sun was born. There grows the peyote, the hikuri, a sacred cactus that is gathered in ceremony and is not taken lightly. The pilgrimage retraces the path of the ancestors, and the drawings of the nierika tell what happens along the way.

Look for the deer. He is called Kauyumari, the blue deer, and he is the one who guides the pilgrims and connects the gods with people. Do you remember the deer tracks carved in the stone of the North Hall? Here the deer is a sacred being. For the Wixárika, maize, deer and peyote are one and the same; in the story, the deer becomes peyote. It is an idea that joins hunting, planting and vision.

Look for the fire. He is called Tatewari, Our Grandfather Fire, and he is the oldest of the ancestors. You have already seen fire as an old and central god: [Huehuetéotl](mna_s04_huehueteotl), in Teotihuacán, and Curicaueri, the god of the Purépecha. Different peoples, in distant places, placed a sacred fire at the heart of the world. Here it is still burning.

The person who leads the ceremonies and sings the stories is usually called a shaman, though in their language he is the marakame, the singer. He spends years learning the chants, which can last entire nights, and he is the keeper of the people’s memory. His visions are the source of many nierikas, and that is why it is said that the painting is not made by the hand alone.

There is a detail about the gaze. The Wixárika do not separate the useful from the sacred: a board, a thread and a little wax make an object of prayer. When you look at the drawings, notice how many symbols repeat: the deer, the sun, the flowers. They repeat because in every vision the same beings return, like a song that is sung again and again.

The Gran Nayar is not a postcard from the past. Its inhabitants defend their mountains and their sacred desert today, and these paintings are their way of explaining it to anyone who wants to listen.

texto: Look for the blue deer among the drawings
Find the peyote flowers and the sun
Notice how each thread is pressed right next to the other on the board

texto.Region: Gran Nayar (Jalisco, Nayarit, Durango and Zacatecas / Wirikuta)
texto.Technique/Material: Polychrome wool yarn attached with beeswax on a wooden board
texto.Function: Devotional painting, portal of mystical vision, and mythological record

texto.pregunta: Myth: Wixárika yarn paintings are just crafts for tourists.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They come from the Wixárika religious tradition: they are offerings and accounts of visions. They have also become a form of art that many families live on.
